items.title: PearlBone gets FDA clearance for world's largest orthopaedic market
paras: The PearlBone FDA approval follows years of testing, evaluation and development. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls )
A bone graft substitute made from Kimberley pearl shells has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Adminstration (FDA).
The product is the first of its kind to repair bone fractures using nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl.
Marine Biomedical says there is more to be done before the product can treat patients, but regulatory approval is an important first step.
Mother-of-pearl harvested in Western Australia's north could soon be used to fill bone fractures for patients in the United States.
WA biotech company Marine Biomedical has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its bone graft substitute, PearlBone.
A manufacturing facility for PearlBone was built in Broome in 2022. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar )
The product is the first of its kind to be developed from nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl.
The iridescent material has been used for ornamental items, jewellery and even buttons.
But Marine Biomedical chief executive Rolee Kumar said it was also effective for bone repair and regeneration.
PearlBone will be used to repair bone fractures for patients in the United States. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar )
"The material of what the mother-of-pearl is made out of, all of these are actually building blocks of our bone too," she said.
"So in a way, it's not surprising when we do these studies we see PearlBone facilitates bone healing."
The United States is the world's largest orthopaedics market, with the bone grafts and substitutes sector valued at $US1.1 billion ($1.5 billion).
Ms Kumar said FDA clearance was an important first step in entering the US market, but there were more hurdles to be overcome before it could be sold.
Rolee Kumar says PearlBone is as safe and effective as existing bone repair materials. ( Supplied: Rolee Kumar )
"We've gone through a process where PearlBone was compared against another existing bone graft that's established itself in the market," she said.
"We've been able to demonstrate PearlBone is as safe and efficacious as the predicate device ."
She said the company also hoped to bring the product to Australian customers in future and expand into other treatments like dental work.
Marine Biomedical was established in 2021 through a partnership with local Broome pearling business Willie Creek Pearls and research expertise from the University of Western Australia (UWA).
Paul Birch says shells are prepped at the farm before being transported to the manufacturing facility in Broome. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls )
Willie Creek chief executive Paul Birch said the collaboration was an exciting opportunity for the pearling industry.
"And with more research, there might be other parts of the oyster that can be used for other biomedical technologies."
The shells farmed by Willie Creek for pearl production undergo cleaning and preparations before being transported to the Marine Biomedical manufacturing facility in Broome.
Mr Birch said there was an abundance of pearl shell available at the farm to meet current requirements, but this could change as the product demand increased.
"So hopefully at one point in time, it might be something the entire industry is able to be involved in and supply to Marine Biomedical," he said.
The shell is harvested at Willie Creek Pearls, off the Kimberley coast. ( Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls )
UWA biomedical and health innovation director Kevin Pfleger said it was an exciting time for medical research in WA.
The professor said it was common for products to gain approval in the United States market before returning to Australia.
"One of the big reasons is because even though we're a very large country geographically, we've got a relatively small population," Professor Pfleger said.
"So if we get approval in the US first, it means it's much more economically viable for us to then come back and market in Australia."
Willie Creek Pearls, based on the outskirts of Broome in WA's north, will provide the product for PearlBone. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins )
Professor Pfleger said the clearance was an "inspiring" achievement for others in the industry.
"The next point is obviously making sales, getting patients and benefiting from that and getting surgeons using it," he said.

items.title: The Townsville creatives making their own queer community
paras: Michael Smith and Lij Bolden found the community they had been looking for through CROOKED. (Image: Emma Jones, ABC North Queensland) ( ABC News: Emma Jones )
Townsville is known for humidity, rugby league, and its unofficial status as North Queensland's capital.
Its queer culture is less visible, but that is changing as more people create the communities they once had to leave regional Queensland to find.
The professional dancer grew up in Gladstone before moving to Brisbane.
"Growing up as a queer person in a regional place, I didn't have any elders or community members to paint a picture of what a queer life could be," they said.
Mx Smith grew up in Gladstone before moving to Brisbane, but later returned to regional Queensland. ( ABC News: Isabella Garrido )
"There's actually a really large queer and trans community in Townsville," they said.
"There just aren't many things that are overtly visible that bring everyone together."
Finding a queer community did not necessarily mean Mx Smith found where they felt most at home.
Rather than leave, they began wondering how else a queer community could look.
With writer P. Eldridge, they created CROOKED, an independent queer publication — due to launch on November 14 — rooted in Gurambilbarra, the traditional Wulgurukaba name for Townsville.
The project quickly revealed there were others also looking for a different way to connect.
Lij Bolden participated in writing workshops to prepare their written piece for CROOKED. ( ABC News: Emma Jones )
Writing for CROOKED gave Mx Bolden the chance to tramp down memory lane.
"It's peppered [with] vignettes of my life and realising I'm queer and discovering other people like me," they said.
"I got to sit in that space and relive my queerness in a place where I did feel lonely and unseen, but realising that maybe I've had that queerness in me this entire time," Mx Bolden said.
"With the amount of political divisiveness and extremity in the world, it takes effort to be neutral," Mx Smith said.
That risk became reality at a Townsville Pride event in June 2025, where Mx Smith was preparing to perform when a small group disrupted the event.
"It had been a long time since I had felt that kind of hostility targeted towards a specific group of people," Mx Smith said.
The experience reinforced for them why visible signs of safety mattered.
"As a young queer person in a regional place, you can be hypervigilant in public, constantly assessing every room you step into, looking for danger and looking for safety," they said.
"If someone has gone to the effort of putting up a [pride] flag, it takes a little of that social anxiety and pressure off your shoulders."
Queensland Council for LGBTI Health chief executive Rebecca Reynolds agreed visible signs of welcome mattered but said what followed was just as important.
Rebecca Reynolds says belonging also means having room to be the whole of who you are. ( Supplied: Queensland Council for LGBTI Health )
"Visible inclusion needs to lead to something people can use: a welcoming person, clear information, an activity they can join or help reaching the right support," she said.
Research suggests knowing a community exists is not necessarily the same as feeling part of it.
A 2025 University of Southern Queensland study of 87 LGBTQ+ people in the Toowoomba region found participants wanted safety, support, acceptance, friendship and connection.
Ms Reynolds said everyday recreational groups could foster connection across the year, beyond larger moments of visibility such as pride events.
"These spaces can take many forms, shaped by the people who use them. What matters is that people can find somewhere that feels right for them."
Writer P. Eldridge helped create CROOKED, an independent queer publication. ( Supplied: P. Eldridge )
"I'm deeply suspicious of the idea that interesting queer culture only happens in capital cities because it doesn't," they said.
"Gurambilbarra has its own queer histories, its own ways of surviving and making community that I think we, as a culture and a movement, can benefit from listening to.
"CROOKED came from wanting to listen to that rather than parachuting in with an idea of what regional queer life should look like."
Ms Eldridge said trans and queer writing had its own lineage, one that was still being defined, shaped and expanded.
"I believe that means there's no reason to confine ourselves. We can pretty much make anything new whenever we want," they said.

"I don't want to mitigate how dangerous regional life can be because of the backward turn toward fascism, but I will say that in the midst of so many crises, there is even more strength, solidarity and hope."
CROOKED, an independent queer publication, is due to launch on November 14. ( Supplied )
Mx Smith said they felt a responsibility to make visible what they could not see growing up.

items.title: Predicting weather in the Southern Hemisphere is challenging. Here's why
paras: Weather forecasts have become much more reliable over the past century. ( ABC )
Atmospheric scientists such as Kimberley Reid from the University of Melbourne face a number of unique challenges that make observing weather trickier here than in the Northern Hemisphere.
"The Northern Hemisphere has … so much more land mass. There's more people and more funding for observations, and more major cities," Dr Reid said.
"In the Southern Hemisphere … we don't have as many surface observations, or as many weather balloons, which are all necessary for working out what's going on."
Despite this, in recent years the Southern Hemisphere has narrowed the forecasting gap, with accuracy that almost matches our northern counterparts.
This isn't due to extra weather stations or balloons but rather an increase in data provided by international satellites, according to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM).
Accurate forecasting can lead to more time to prepare, which can help save lives. ( ABC News: Tahlia Davis )
While this has provided a wealth of data for weather forecasting around the world, experts warn that satellites can't help forecast everything.
And as weather gets more extreme, forecasters are turning to new technologies and techniques to keep up.
Humans have been trying to predict the weather for thousands of years , but it's only in the last few decades that forecasters could peer into the future with any kind of certainty.
Short-term forecasts between one and three days are reasonably accurate, but the further into the future the forecast looks — up to five or so days — the less dependable they are.
According to Dr Reid, this is because weather is particularly chaotic, and tiny variables can end up having "large flow-on effects" over just a couple of days.
This has historically been the case in the Southern Hemisphere where Dr Reid said there just isn't enough land for equipment.
This lack of data was visible in the historical accuracy gap between the two hemispheres.
In the 1980s, a three-day forecast was about 90 per cent accurate in the Northern Hemisphere, but just over 80 per cent in the Southern Hemisphere.
Michael Logan, general manager of decision support services at the BOM, said this improved over the next two decades, but the Southern Hemisphere still lagged behind into the 2000s.
The introduction of data from specialised weather satellites helped close the gap.
Australia doesn’t have its own weather satellites, but instead uses data from 40 satellites owned by countries including the US and Japan.
While some satellites orbit the Earth, others stay above one location by following the planet's rotation.
The copious amount of globally shared information produced by these satellites is vital for groups like the BOM, providing more than 90 per cent data for weather forecasts.
Weather satellites like Japan's Himawari 8 and 9 are very important for modern weather forecasting. ( Wikimedia: Himawari89 / Japan Meteorological Agency / CC BY 4.0 )
"For the Bureau, even just what we use in our weather predictions, it's of the order of 13.5–14 million observations every day coming in from these satellites," Mr Logan said.
"That's contributed an enormous amount of data that really helps with the numerical computing models."
But according to Martin Jucker, an atmospheric climate scientist at the University of New South Wales, many of the satellites are coming towards the end of their life.
"The really big [worry] is new satellites that were supposed to replace old ones have been cancelled," Dr Jucker said.
"So these satellites will reach their end of life and replacements will be late."
Forecasting extreme weather events has become increasingly important as the world's climate changes.
"We're making sure that we're improving the skill of predicting the big weather events, whether it be cyclones or really extreme rainfall or extreme heat," Mr Logan said.
Along with using satellite data, forecasters are turning to AI to hone their models.
BOM, for example, already uses Google DeepMind's forecasting system for cyclones.
In 2024, the system was shown to predict the weather 15 days ahead and more accurately than the best system currently in use.
Despite advances in AI, accurately predicting some extreme weather phenomena is still a major challenge .
Dr Reid's research focuses on atmospheric rivers, which produce large amounts of rainfall or snowfall over a region when they hit land.
"An atmospheric river is a long, narrow region of enhanced water vapour transport in the lower atmosphere," she said.
Understanding when and where weather patterns created by atmospheric rivers will hit well in advance can help limit damage and casualties.
In 2022, an atmospheric river caused both the Brisbane and Lismore floods .
"Having more observational data has the potential to improve the timing and location of extreme rainfall forecasts so that people have plenty of time to evacuate if needed."
Hurricane hunter planes are able to get much more information than a satellite or weather station. ( Wikimedia: Lieutenant Commander Andrew Utama/NOAA Corps/Public Domain )
In the US, air crews known as hurricane hunters, fly airplanes directly through atmospheric rivers to gain data.
This extreme close-up information can be used alongside satellite data and modelling to provide more accurate forecasts.
"They ' ve got some good results showing these improved observations improve [forecasting for] where and when these atmospheric rivers will hit," Dr Reid said.
"The more information you have at the present time, the better your forecast will be."

items.title: Minns vows to open 100 long-day childcare centres if re-elected
paras: The Minns government has committed to building and opening 100 long-day childcare centres ( ABC News: Lucas Hill )
The NSW Labor government has pledged to open 100 new long-day childcare centres if re-elected in March.
It is on top of an existing promise from the Minns government to build and open 100 new preschools by January.
The government expects 8,000 families will benefit from 5,000 new placements at long-day childcare centres.
The NSW government will open and operate 100 new long-day childcare centres to address demand if it wins the state election in March.
The centres are in addition to an existing government pledge to build 100 new preschools and have them operational from January next year.
In the private sector, long-day centres offer early childhood services for children from birth to four years old and operate between 7am and 6pm.
The announcement on Saturday from the Minns government will deliver the first publicly owned long-day childcare centres in NSW, providing 5,000 places for about 8,000 families.
Chris Minns expects many long-day centre locations to open up in Western Sydney. ( ABC News )
Premier Chris Minns said the centres would be built on existing public primary school sites and in areas deemed so-called childcare deserts.
He said the government would "not be indiscriminate" about new locations and that he expected many to open in Western Sydney and regional NSW.
"The reality is, for us in New South Wales, if we want a productive economy, we want to make sure that we're giving every family the opportunity to get ahead," Mr Minns said.
Prue Car says families are in desperate need of extended child care hours. ( ABC News )
Deputy Premier Prue Car said families desperately needed the extended care hours the centres would provide.
"That will end the double drop off and it will make it easier for parents to get back into the workforce," she said.
"It will also create an opportunity for high quality early learning as children transition into kindergarten and primary school."
The government will also extend the transitional funding period for community run preschools.
As part of the NSW government's early childhood education reforms, the Universal Preschool Funding Program will replace the Start Strong arrangement from January 1.

But community preschool operators, which are not-for-profit, expressed concern earlier in the week that the new funding model would affect the quality of care and leave some centres financially worse off.
According to the government, 10,000 families are missing out on community preschool places.
" We have listened to the concerns of the sector, and we've responded to that by guaranteeing their funding for two years," Mr Minns said on Saturday.
"So that will give community preschools a funding guarantee that they will not go backwards while we work with them on how we can get more children into their high quality preschool."

items.title: Do Australians actually want cheaper housing? We're finding out fast
paras: Australia's housing crisis has entered new territory. ( ABC News: John Gunn )
Australia's housing crisis has entered a new phase: a little less conversation, a little more action.

The first seeds were planted three years ago, with a landmark national agreement to build more homes. The target, 1.2 million in five years, is likely doomed. But what mattered was that a target was set at all. After years of lip service, leaders had promised to act on the root cause.

Then there was last year's economic roundtable. After much fanfare, the closed-door event had seemed like a fizzer. But for Treasurer Jim Chalmers, it helped build the case that Labor's old policy to wind back negative gearing could be reinvented, and framed as a leg up for home buyers over investors.

A policy to boost supply and a policy to slash demand. Throw in the highest interest rates in 18 years, and all of a sudden a housing market that seemed as if it would never turn is turning very fast indeed. This week saw the steepest drop-off in new home loans ever recorded.

Commentators had long wondered whether, for all the hand-wringing about the housing crisis, Australians would actually want a solution when it came, since, one way or another, cheaper homes for the young can only mean less valuable homes for those who already own them.

But no more need to wonder: we're finding out. A tumbling market may not have been federal Labor's ideal pathway to affordable housing, but after months of dithering, the government took a tentative step this week towards embracing the chaos, framing it as a win for homebuyers.

In the coming weeks and months, Labor governments in Australia's two largest states will put their own higher-density plans to voters. At federal and state levels, Liberals are betting voters will dislike the prescribed cure worse than the sickness.

Labor did not expect its changes to the capital gains tax and negative gearing to tank house prices. Treasury analysis predicted prices would still grow, but by 2 per cent less. Chalmers has repeatedly said he is "not targeting a particular price".
Nor did it want prices to tank. In 2024, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said it was her "strong view" that falling prices would be bad.
"Our policies are not going to reduce house prices. We want house prices to grow sustainably," she said then.
Clare O'Neil has been caught between championing affordability and protecting people's investments. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson )

But now they have fallen. The median national house price is 5.6 per cent below its March peak, and 3.9 per cent for apartments. The drop-off has been sharper in Melbourne and Sydney, and some analysts predict double-digit declines.

Other indicators point in the same direction. The auction clearance rate has plunged below 50 per cent, compared to its long-run average of 60 per cent. And new figures this week showed a record 15 per cent dip in new loans between June and September.

The chill was evident across the board, but it was clearly worse for investors (31 per cent) than for homebuyers (5 per cent). First home buyers (8 per cent) fared worse than established homebuyers, but still far better than investors.

High rates have clearly played a role. But they do not explain why investors are falling away by "so much more than in previous interest rate increasing cycles", as Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock observed last week.
"[That] suggests something else is going on here, and [that] is the tax changes," she said. In other words, the tax changes are doing what they were designed to do: discourage investors.

Until this week, the government had been skittish about embracing that. Even after opinion polls suggested a majority of Australians believed that prices needed to fall, ministers were nervous about embracing the nosedive.
"We've had a housing market geared towards investors for a generation, and where did it get us? Plummeting ownership, out-of-control house price increases, and a generation losing hope," she said.

"These numbers show the balance is shifting back … It is absolutely the case that volumes are down, as you would expect in a period where prices are softening. But these figures also clearly show a strong shift away from investors and towards Australians buying a home to live in."

It is a risky gambit. First home buyers may be getting a leg up — CBA's Matt Comyn said yesterday their share of new loan applications doubled last month. But a fast-falling market is a risky one to enter, especially with high rates, and it can also chill housing supply.
Liberal housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg seized on the comments, calling them "strange".
"People would look at what Clare O'Neil says and think, 'Well, what planet is she living on? Why is she saying fewer loans is good?' Fewer loans is bad [sic]. We need to see more lending."

A chorus of real estate moguls and personal finance celebrities agree. A prominent example is podcaster Mark Bouris, who predicted in The Australian this week "the longest downturn in our history" and warned: "We're going to have a serious structural hit to people's wealth."
The comments are revealing, hinting at what motivates many critics. Not affordability, but wealth.
That cannot be said of Bragg, one of a handful of politicians who have publicly embraced the idea that lower house prices could be welcome if they happen via a supply boom, not a demand chill.
But for many home owners, wealth is front of mind, and this is just as true on the supply side as it is on the demand side, as state governments are finding out.

In Victoria, the Labor government has pursued the most aggressively pro-supply policy in the country, designating several Melbourne suburban hubs as so-called "activity centres", where high-density towers will be allowed in narrow strips and medium density in wider surrounds.

Typical of the cynical political style of former premier Daniel Andrews and his successor Jacinta Allan, many zones are in places Labor will never win, including in Brighton and state Liberal leader Jess Wilson's Kew.
Jess Wilson said a Coalition government would shift the focus of high-rise development to Melbourne's CBD and inner city. ( ABC News )
Locals have been whipped into a frenzy by dystopian artists' impressions of amorphous black skyscrapers invading their leafy shopping strips, a feature of media coverage.
Kew and Brighton will hardly shape the election, which pundits predict Labor will lose for other reasons, but Wilson has vowed to scrap the plan and give local councils a veto if elected.

A similar dynamic is emerging in Sydney, where the Minns Labor government will face voters early in the new year and where designated density zones in suburbs like Woollahra and Crows Nest are also opposed by the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane.
Sloane, echoing Wilson and many Teal MPs, says she supports more housing but frames her complaint as one of consultation and is also promising a council veto.

The argument has a reasonable-sounding guise — "We just want locals to have a say" — but to pro-supply campaigners like Peter Tulip, it is an all-too-familiar smokescreen for building fewer homes, since councils make decisions for existing residents, not potential new ones.

"[The] households who move in would be better off. As would renters and homebuyers who benefit from improved affordability. They greatly outnumber the opponents, but they don't get to vote for the local politicians who are biased against new housing," he said last week.

If Tulip is right, the political numbers game should favour Labor governments at federal and state levels if their policies really do make housing more affordable: they would lose Kew and Crows Nest, but win the country.
In different economic and political circumstances, that reckoning might have come gradually. Instead, we are hurtling towards it.

items.title: Former NT administrator opens up about being groomed as a child
paras: The Northern Territory's former administrator says the next generation of children need to be kept safe. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )
Hugh Heggie was just 14 years old when an older church youth group leader began grooming him.
The youth group in Victoria, where he grew up, had been a safe place. Then one evening, the leader — a man in his 20s — offered him alcohol and suggested the pair go to the drive-in cinema.
Two days later, the man asked him to go to the drive-in again, and this time he relented and asked his mother for permission.

Now aged 76, Mr Heggie is a former doctor and the former Northern Territory administrator — the NT's equivalent of a state governor — who became a household name during the COVID pandemic as the NT's chief health officer.
More than 60 years after his experience with the youth group leader, he is telling his story publicly for the first time.
Hugh Heggie was the NT's chief health officer during COVID. ( ABC News: Che Chorley )
On that day, Mr Heggie said the church leader picked him up and kept offering him alcohol.
"I realised he was trying to get me intoxicated, so I pretended to drink," he said.
Halfway through the film, Mr Heggie alleged the man put his hand on his leg.
"When his hand went too far, I got out of the car and said, 'You either take me home now or I will walk home'," he said.
Mr Heggie never returned to the youth group, nor did he report the incident to police or tell his parents.
He said he considered himself lucky to have escaped, and chose to bury what happened, telling no one for decades.
He said family members were sexually assaulted and, as a doctor, other men disclosed their own instances of abuse in the privacy of a consultation room.
As a parent he became hypervigilant, worrying about sending his children to Scouts or friends' homes.
He recalled refusing to let one of his children attend a party in a park.
Hugh Heggie says he never reported what happened to him, but it affected how he acted as a parent. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish )
"Other times, dropping my young adult [child] off, I said, 'I'm going to come in and introduce myself to the family' … and I often parked outside so I was there to take her home," he said.
"But yes, it does worry me … particularly because of the possibility there were other young people that he took advantage of."
Clare Leaney says stories like Hugh Heggie's can empower other people to seek justice. ( Supplied: National Survivors' Foundation )
Instances of child harm have surged across Australia in the past decade , according to recent research by the University of Sydney.
However, National Survivors Foundation chief executive Clare Leaney said stories like Mr Heggie's were crucial for changing these statistics and empowering people to seek justice.
"Hugh is an example of survivorship that people don't necessarily expect to see," she said.
"Of how survivors [can] build a life that can be both surviving and thriving [despite] the most horrific violence imaginable."
Hugh Heggie swore in Lia Finocchiaro as NT chief minister at Government House in 2024 during his time as the NT administrator. ( Supplied: Pema Pakhrin/NT News )
Although more people now speak out, Ms Leaney said gaps in the law remained a barrier.

She said in all states and territories except for Victoria and the ACT, organisations including churches, Scouts and swim clubs could not be held vicariously liable for abuse committed by individuals who were not employees, potentially limiting survivors' avenues for compensation and justice.
"Justice should not be dependent on a person's employment status," she said.
NT Attorney General Marie-Clare Boothby said the government "will work with national counterparts on a uniform approach to redress and liability" and urged survivors to seek support and justice.
"It takes immense courage to disclose abuse and sexual violence, and I encourage victim-survivors to contact NT Police and to access specialist advice and support."
Mr Heggie is now an ambassador for the National Survivors Foundation, and said he hoped sharing his story would help other survivors feel less alone.
"It's important that we all have an understanding of what occurs, to prevent it," he said.
"We need to provide hope for the next generation … and make sure the next generation of children are safe.
"The metric of that will be whether the numbers of sexual assaults is reduced."

items.title: Police seeking witnesses after violent home invasion in Canberra
paras: Police asked anyone with information to come forward as investigations continue into the October incident. ( Supplied: ACT Policing )
Investigations are continuing into a violent home invasion in Canberra's inner north suburb of Hackett last month, where a woman holding a child was threatened at knifepoint.
ACT Policing said about 11pm on Monday October 5, three men, armed with a firearm, knife, sword and a baseball bat, forced entry to a home on Harris Place, and demanded money from the woman.
It's alleged one of the men struck her in the head, before the group stole cash and a Mercedes Benz sedan.
They urged anyone who saw suspicious activity in the area on October 5, or who otherwise has information, to contact Crime Stoppers, with the option to share information anonymously.

items.title: Family-run berry farm looks to AI and automation to ease workforce challenges
paras: Blueberries are a popular fruit across Australia and Asia. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
WA's largest blueberry grower is investing in AI, automation and machine harvesting as it expands production.
The business says automation can help reduce labour costs, but will not replace a need for workers.
Western Berry plans to triple its production and explore AI-guided pruning.

Western Australia's largest blueberry grower is turning to artificial intelligence and autonomous technology to reduce labour costs and ease the challenge of finding enough workers during the peak harvest period.

Earlier this year, Australia's food producers raised concerns about the federal government's slower visa processing times and limits on working holiday maker numbers, saying the changes could reduce access to seasonal labour.
WA's largest blueberry farm is ramping up production. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
Western Berry's blueberry operation is 100 kilometres north of Perth and spans 120 hectares.
This year it will produce just under 1,500 tonnes of blueberries bound for supermarkets across Australia and Asia.
Its owners, the Kwiecien-Fisher family, are in a significant expansion phase and hope to triple production in the coming years.
Derek Fisher and Marek Kwiecien-Fisher at Western Berry. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
But producing more fruit will also require more workers, something many horticultural businesses say is becoming increasingly difficult and expensive.
An autonomous foliar sprayer moves through the blueberry plants. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
The family hopes innovations like driverless tractors, machine harvesting and eventually artificial intelligence will help ease the challenges.
Operations manager Marek Kwiecien-Fisher said the company was trialling autonomous technology as much as it could on the property.

It is using driverless, self-navigating tractors to do foliar spraying of the berries and laser-guided "green on brown" weed control on the ground, and to perform tasks such as hauling berries from the field to the pack house.
A driverless tractor makes its way to the pack house. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
"Then in the packing we use a lot of autonomy in photographic packing, grading solutions and autonomous punnetising," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.

With autonomous technology now more accessible than ever, farmers across various food industries are determining how self-guided machinery can fit into their businesses, and the balance between people and machines on the farm.
Marek Kwiecien-Fisher says the company is trialling new technology. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
Driverless tractors use GPS mapping, sensors and cameras to navigate predetermined routes and can also be operated remotely.
Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said they were an expensive outlay and time consuming when learning how to set up and operate, but he believed they had a firm future on the farm.

"Even things that we didn't think that we were gaining data on has the ability to show us how we'll operate next year, and what areas we could fill the gaps in, either our production or our supply models or our customer requirements," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.
Blueberries are photographed six to nine times before they make their way into these rows, ready to be put into punnets. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said future options for technology use on the property could go as far as humanoid robots pruning plants and AI modelling of future crops.

"If we can teach an AI model where to prune and how to prune, and if that can teach a humanoid robot where to prune and how to prune, you basically get rid of any damage to your drip lines, trellising, your pruning equipment, your plants and it becomes a very precise farming technique," he said.
"The pruning basically sets how much fruit we're going to pick next year, so it's one of the largest indicators of how we can forecast our volumes and our production for the coming season.
"We're [also] looking at autonomous mowing, flower counts and crop health detection systems, so cameras that look at the crop [can] check for poor irrigation."
Western Berry is a family business on a rapid growth trajectory. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
While technology is playing an increasingly important role in the business, Western Berry remains firmly family-run.
Almost 30 years ago Derek Fisher and his wife Barbara wanted space for their young family and purchased what is now one part of the farm.
Derek Fisher says there is strong global demand for Australian blueberries. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )

It was a former ostrich property that they initially planted with olives in 2001, but a successful trial of one hectare of blueberries resulted in them changing course and moving into the blueberry industry.

Now their three sons, Adam, Marek and Tom Kwiecien-Fisher, run the business. Adam is in charge of supply chain and packing, Tom oversees the design and construction of new farm areas, and Marek manages operations.
Adam Kwiecien-Fisher manages supply-chain logistics. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
In 2021, the family struck an agreement with global agricultural company United Exports and Oz Varieties, giving them access to the unique OZblu blueberry genetics.
Ripe berries fall off the plant easily, but not before they are ready, which is key for successful machine harvesting.
Tom Kwiecien-Fisher manages the design and construction of new farm areas. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
The property is working with two harvesters. The latest model is battery-operated, solar-powered and controlled via remote control, collecting fruit and stacking trays by itself.
"Eventually, we will be using AI learning to make this machine autonomous so we can press a button and it drives itself," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.
The latest model blueberry harvester will eventually move autonomously along the the row of plants. ( ABC Mid West and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
A harvesting machine can pick up to 6 tonnes of blueberries a day at a cost of about 50 cents a kilogram, compared with about $6 a kilogram for hand picking.
He said machinery and autonomous technology service provision was creating a new employment industry within agriculture.
"There's a huge opportunity for computer science specialists, people that actually understand how to operate AI, people that understand how to operate those machines."
Quoc Thanh Cao is known as the fastest blueberry picker on the property. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis )
But Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said at most half of their crop would be machine harvested, and pickers remained a very important asset to the business.
Western Berry employs more than 200 people to pick its crop, making it one of the largest employers in the region.

"We are growing at a rate and expanding at a rate that our full employment numbers are growing faster than tech is replacing jobs, and just because we have tech doesn't mean that workers aren't required," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.

items.title: Reserve Bank of India imposes monetary penalty on One Mobikwik Systems Limited
paras: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 06, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹9.00 lakh (Rupees Nine Lakh only) on One Mobikwik Systems Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of the directions issued by RBI on ‘Prepaid Payment lnstruments (PPIs)’ and ‘Fraud reporting’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under the provisions of section 30(1) read with section 26(6) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its operations for the period from June 2025 to March 2026. Based on supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for its failure to comply with the said RBI directions. After considering the company’s reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: the company had allowed fund transfer by certain PPI holders to non-pre-registered beneficiaries beyond the prescribed limit. the company failed to report certain frauds within the prescribed timeline. The action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1496

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. Winners ranged from corporate giants like Aditya Birla Group and Accenture to global educators and community leaders. items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: India sends humanitarian aid to Palestine; consignment comprises 30 tons of essential items

This initial consignment comprises 30 tons of essential items, including medicines, surgical supplies, dental products, general medical items, and high-energy biscuits, which will be distributed through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA). Sharing a post on X, Randhir Jaiswal, the official spokesperson of the Ministry of External Affairs wrote, "India sends humanitarian assistance for the people of Palestine through UNRWA." "The first tranche of assistance comprising 30 tons of medicine and food items has departed today. The consignment includes a wide range of essential medicines and surgical supplies, dental products, general medical items and high-energy biscuits," the post added.

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry.
